column1: A Monitoring Framework At Layer4-7 Granularity Using Network Service Headers
column6: Network monitoring within highly dynamic, virtualized, and programmable networks. The authors argue that traditional traffic mirroring is too rigid and carries excessive overhead for modern, softwarized architectures. They contend that embedding monitoring metadata directly into active traffic flows offers a far more granular, flexible, and standardized alternative to traditional physical-virtual monitoring gaps.
column7: To design and evaluate a monitoring framework that leverages Network Service Headers (NSH) to embed tracking metadata (such as packet coloring and timestamping) directly into traffic flows, enabling operators to measure fine-grained Layer 4-7 metrics (e.g., jitter and delay) with minimal overhead.
column8: The research approach employs a standardization-driven design paradigm to embed monitoring metadata directly into active traffic flows rather than using traditional, rigid traffic mirroring. The methodology involves deploying a unified monitoring framework that leverages the Network Service Header (NSH) to execute packet coloring, timestamping, and packet interception at Layers 4 through 7, enabling operators to analyze fine-grained metrics such as jitter and delay across physical and virtual infrastructures with minimal overhead.
column9: DPI classifiers, virtual probes (implemented in experiments); Firewalls, NAT, video transcoders, caches, load balancers, virus scanners, content filters, proxies, WAN accelerators, charging applications (cited as examples).
column10: Virtual Machines, Open vSwitch.
column11: Runtime monitoring and troubleshooting.
column12: Integrated within a Service Function Chaining (SFC) architecture using Network Service Headers (NSH) where ingress classifiers mark packets with Layer 4-7 metadata and downstream virtual probes consume and modify these headers on-the-fly under SDN controller coordination.
column14: Physical and virtual network probes placed strategically along service function paths, including ingress classifiers, service function forwarders, virtual switches, deep packet inspection engines, and egress telemetry collectors.
column15: Packet counts, packet volume, packet loss rates, latency, delay, jitter, relative packet arrival ordering, timestamps, and connectivity status.
column19: Network Service Headers (NSH) with MD-type=0x2 TLV metadata encodings, OpenFlow, Open vSwitch.
column24: Evaluated throughput loss and latency overhead of the proposed NSH marking method against a baseline without monitoring and a traditional traffic mirroring setup (vProbe). In Test Setup 1 with four Iperf clients sending TCP traffic to a server, NSH header stamping achieved normalized throughput of 84.25% to 84.75% compared to the baseline, performing 2.25% to 6.31% lower than traffic mirroring which reached 86.76% to 90.97%. In Test Setup 2 with Open vSwitch NSH timestamp metadata adding 64-bit timestamps at six intermediate points, throughput overhead was approximately 7% for both 10 MB and 100 MB flows. Latency impact was minimal: 64-byte packets increased from 0.514 ms to 0.530 ms, while 1000-byte packets increased from 0.532 ms to 0.535 ms with 0% packet loss.
column25: Limitations explicitly stated by the authors note that the evaluation setup was executed on a single physical server, meaning throughput values represent relative overhead metrics rather than absolute network performance across distributed hardware setups. Methodological limitations include relying on synthetic Iperf flow generation rather than operational enterprise or carrier traffic profiles.
column26: Explicitly identified by the authors, the real-world performance, accuracy limits, and scalability of NSH metadata marking across complex, multi-hop service function chains remain unquantified. Inferred from the article, the impact of NSH header manipulation on hardware-accelerated middleboxes and legacy non-NSH-aware network functions requires further investigation.
column27: The authors concluded that embedding monitoring metadata into the IETF Network Service Header provides a flexible, standardized framework for Layer 4 to Layer 7 flow classification and troubleshooting across physical and virtual domains with acceptable throughput and latency overhead. Future work proposed by the authors includes evaluating performance across specific operational use cases, building and deploying an intent-based monitoring engine and northbound APIs, and evaluating open-source testbed implementations to determine if additional instrumentation is needed in SDN controllers and protocols for closed-loop network control.

column1: Policy-Based Monitoring And Energy Management For Nfv Data Centers
column6: Energy efficiency and dynamic resource management in virtualized data centers. The authors argue that massive power waste can be mitigated by dynamically monitoring resource consumption (such as bandwidth and memory) and consolidating workloads. They argue that dividing management policies into hard constraints (for stability) and soft constraints (for optimization) allows for significant energy savings without compromising network function performance.
column7: To develop a domain-agnostic policy engine that guides automated, linear-programming-based virtual machine (VM) migration to consolidate tasks and deactivate idle hardware, optimizing energy use while meeting Service Level Agreement (SLA) demands.
column8: The research approach is a simulation-backed systems optimization paradigm that designs a domain-agnostic policy engine to orchestrate energy efficiency in virtualized data centers. The methodology integrates dynamic resource consumption monitoring (specifically memory and bandwidth) with linear programming to guide automated virtual machine (VM) migrations, distinguishing between hard constraints for stability and soft constraints for optimization to consolidate workloads onto fewer servers and deactivate idle hardware under an OpenStack cloud environment.
column9: Parental control, IDS/IPS (implemented in simulations).
column10: OpenStack (Nova, Ceilometer, Heat, Congress).
column11: Runtime resource orchestration and dynamic workload migration.
column12: VNFs are placed in virtual machines on physical hosts where dynamic memory telemetry is collected by Ceilometer and evaluated against soft/hard policies in Congress, triggering a linear programming placement solver to migrate VMs and consolidate servers to deactivate idle hardware.
column14: OpenStack infrastructure monitoring and analytics subsystems, specifically OpenStack Ceilometer and OpenStack Nova drivers collecting compute, storage, and network metrics across data center hosts and virtual machines.
column15: CPU utilization, average memory utilization, maximum memory capacity, network bandwidth utilization across server interfaces and switch interconnects, host utilization percentages, and server power consumption in watts.
column19: OpenStack Ceilometer.
column24: Evaluated policy-based energy management using linear programming optimization integrated with OpenStack components including Ceilometer, Nova, Heat, and Congress. In a test scenario with 16 physical hosts running memory-intensive virtual network function workloads, dynamic monitoring of host underutilization combined with linear programming-driven workload consolidation reduced total power consumption from 1944 Watts across 16 hosts at 10% to 20% utilization down to 743 Watts consolidated onto 3 active hosts at 92.5% to 95% utilization, achieving a 61.78% energy savings by powering off idle hardware.
column25: Limitations explicitly stated by the authors note that the initial implementation focuses exclusively on memory utilization monitoring for memory-intensive virtual network functions, omitting multi-resource joint constraints. Methodological limitations include validating power savings using simulation models and SPEC power profiles rather than live physical power meter measurements under real-world dynamic traffic bursts.
column26: Explicitly identified by the authors, dynamic resource optimization for heterogeneous server environments with non-uniform CPU, memory, and network capabilities or hardware acceleration features remains unaddressed. Inferred from the article, the trade-off between live virtual machine migration energy overhead and service level agreement latency violations during aggressive server consolidation requires deeper empirical quantification.
column27: The authors concluded that combining dynamic soft-constraint monitoring warnings with reactive hard-constraint linear programming optimization significantly improves resource utilization and reduces data center power consumption while avoiding service level agreement degradation. Future work proposed by the authors includes incorporating network bandwidth and CPU utilization constraints into the optimization model, extending the framework to heterogeneous multi-vendor server platforms with hardware acceleration capabilities, and adapting the policy engine to inter-data-center energy and bandwidth optimization combining optical and Ethernet switching.

column1: Vision – Interactive And Selective Visualization For Management Of Nfv- Enabled Networks
column6: Troubleshooting and network management through visual analytics in NFV systems. The authors argue that the transition from physical hardware to virtualized, software-based network functions produces massive, complex datasets that easily overwhelm human administrators. They argue that interactive, selective visualization is necessary to help operators discover subtle issues like placement errors or affinity/anti-affinity violations.
column7: To introduce VISION, a specialized management platform that aggregates NFV environment data and renders it into intuitive, interactive visual formats (such as forwarding graphs, migration timelines, and statistical charts) to facilitate human-driven network troubleshooting.
column8: The research approach follows an interactive visual analytics paradigm designed to bridge the gap between high-level orchestration metrics and the human operator's cognitive capacity during network troubleshooting. The methodology involves building "VISION", a specialized management platform that aggregates complex data from NFV environments and translates them into forwarding graphs, migration histories, and statistical charts, enabling administrators to selectively visualize and isolate placement errors and affinity/anti-affinity violations.
column9: Firewall, Load Balancer, DPI, NAT, DHCP, Video Transcoding (implemented in case studies/experiments).
column10: openMANO framework, openvim.
column11: Runtime monitoring, live migration analysis, and interactive diagnostics.
column12: VNFs are deployed on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware as multi-tenant service chains (forwarding graphs); openMANO orchestrators pull event logs and resource states (CPU, memory, traffic metrics) via REST APIs to populate a visualization engine, highlighting affinity/anti-affinity violations and traffic bottlenecks.
column14: openMANO northbound REST APIs (openvim and openmano for Virtualized Infrastructure Manager, VNF Manager, and Orchestrator telemetry), customized socket-based VNF monitors, and PostgreSQL event databases.
column15: CPU usage, memory usage, memory diagnostics, latency, propagation delay, packet counts, and network bandwidth usage.
column16: Event logs including VNF migration logs, VNF failure logs, SLA disruption alerts, and system event notifications.
column17: Historical sequences of VNF migration logs mapped over time to analyze physical host placements and resource sharing relationships.
column18: The platform correlates real-time CPU, memory, and bandwidth metrics with event logs and historical migration traces by rendering visual line charts of resource metrics directly alongside timeline blocks of migration events and topological forwarding graphs, allowing operators to visually correlate VNF performance degradation with specific migration events and hardware sharing.
column19: openMANO REST APIs.
column24: Developed and validated the VISION platform built with Django, PostgreSQL, and openMANO REST APIs across three virtual network function as a service operational case studies. In the first case study on bottleneck identification, interactive forwarding graph visualizations enabled operators to instantly spot saturated deep packet inspection and network address translation virtual functions co-located on Hardware X whose 100% bandwidth usage degraded forwarding graphs for Tenants 1 and 3 due to improper placement. In the second case study on affinity issues, combining migration history timelines with latency line charts revealed that firewall performance degraded specifically when co-located on the same physical server as a load balancer, leading operators to enforce anti-affinity rules. In the third case study on tenant demands, force-directed graph layouts successfully mapped virtual function and tenant request proximities, demonstrating that a shared firewall was heavily utilized by Tenant 1, justifying instantiation of a dedicated virtual network function.
column25: Limitations explicitly stated by the authors note that the data collector relies on openMANO APIs and does not natively support alternative NFV management frameworks such as ClickOS or openNFV. Methodological limitations include relying on qualitative scenario walkthroughs without quantitative user-study metrics comparing human operators using VISION against traditional command-line or text-log tools.
column26: Explicitly identified by the authors, there is a lack of standardized human-centric evaluation techniques to measure and quantify the visual operational efficiency of management tools in NFV environments. Inferred from the article, visual scalability and graph decluttering mechanisms for ultra-large-scale networks containing tens of thousands of active virtual network functions and complex multi-layer dependencies remain unaddressed.
column27: The authors concluded that combining interactive, selective visualization techniques with management and orchestration telemetry allows operators to quickly discover non-obvious management problems, including hidden resource bottlenecks, hardware anti-affinity conflicts, and tenant usage imbalances. Future work proposed by the authors includes extending VISION with new visual models for conflicting policy detection, service chain verification, and service level agreement tracking, conducting human-centric user evaluations, and supporting additional virtual network function execution environments including ClickOS and openNFV.

column1: An Extensible Autoscaling Engine (Ae) For Software-Based Network Functions
column6: Automated resource scaling within the ETSI NFV architectural framework. The authors argue that static resource allocation fails to maintain service quality under highly fluctuating demand. They contend that a modular, three-tier scaling architecture (detection, decision-making, and execution) is essential to bridge the gap between cloud-native elasticity and strict telecommunications reliability.
column7: To design and implement an extensible Autoscaling Engine (AE) integrated into the Open Baton open-source framework, enabling automated resource lifecycle management for virtualized network functions (such as IP Multimedia Subsystems).
column8: The research approach utilizes an architectural prototyping framework to integrate cloud computing elasticity with strict telecommunications reliability standards. The methodology involves designing a modular, three-tier autoscaling engine (AE) composed of a detector, a decision-maker, and an executor, which is integrated into the Open Baton open-source platform and validated using practical web server and IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) scenarios to automate lifecycle resource management.
column9: Load Balancer, Web Servers, IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS), Home Subscriber Server (HSS) (implemented in experiments).
column10: Open Baton framework.
column11: Runtime autoscaling (dynamic elasticity).
column12: Implemented as a highly available network service consisting of worker VNFCs behind a load balancer; the Autoscaling Engine (AE) integrated with the Open Baton MANO framework uses a generic VNFM and monitoring drivers to check policy thresholds on the VIM and invoke scale-in/scale-out operations through the NFVO.
column14: Open Baton monitoring drivers that monitor virtualized infrastructure and VNF instances.
column15: CPU idle time, CPU utilization percentage, memory utilization, incoming request volume, and request throughput.
column19: Open Baton monitoring driver plugin interface.
column24: Integrated an ETSI NFV-compliant Autoscaling Engine into Open Baton using RabbitMQ AMQP, RPC and REST interfaces, and Zabbix and Ceilometer monitoring drivers. In an HAProxy load-balanced web server evaluation scenario, the Autoscaling Engine dynamically expanded virtual machine instances from 1 to 8 as CPU idle time dropped below 40% over a 30-minute load increase, and subsequently scaled back down to 1 instance as load decreased, maintaining service availability with zero request drops after scaling. Execution timing breakdown showed that scale-out execution required 81.7 seconds, accounting for 99.8% of total scale-out duration due to virtual machine boot times, software package installation, and configuration, while scale-in condition detection to execution completion took 513 ms with actual scale-in execution requiring 344 ms.
column25: Limitations explicitly stated by the authors note that generic threshold-based policy rules require manual parameter tuning per service type and are poorly suited for multi-parameter workload spikes. Methodological limitations include scale-out latency introducing a window of vulnerability where sudden, sharp traffic surges can temporarily overwhelm buffering capacity before new instances finish booting.
column26: Explicitly identified by the authors, static threshold-based scaling rules cannot dynamically adapt to changing traffic patterns across diverse virtual network function types without manual re-configuration. Inferred from the article, proactive predictive scaling models capable of pre-allocating virtual machine instances prior to threshold breach are absent from the architecture.
column27: The authors concluded that integrating an Autoscaling Engine into the ETSI NFV MANO framework delivers dynamic runtime elasticity, maintaining network service stability, availability, and resource efficiency during fluctuating traffic demands. Future work proposed by the authors includes incorporating dynamic machine learning mechanisms into the Detector component to analyze historical traffic patterns and proactively predict peak load triggers for advance scaling.

column1: Sfc-Checker: Checking The Correct Forwarding Behavior Of Service Function Chaining
column6: Verifying the forwarding behavior of Service Function Chains (SFCs). The authors argue that the stateful nature of modern middleboxes (such as firewalls) makes traffic path analysis highly complex. They argue that representing middleboxes through a hybrid model of match-action tables and Finite State Machines (FSMs) allows for rapid, proactive static analysis of network reachability.
column7: To build SFC-Checker, a highly scalable verification tool that models the network as a Stateful Forwarding Graph (SFG) to proactively detect configuration errors and reachability violations in sub-second timeframes before live service outages occur.
column8: The research approach uses a formal verification and static analysis paradigm to model and audit the forwarding paths of complex, stateful middleboxes. The methodology introduces "SFC-Checker", a tool that models service functions through match-action tables and Finite State Machines (FSMs) to construct a Stateful Forwarding Graph (SFG), applying graph-traversal algorithms to proactively identify reachability invariants and configuration errors in sub-second timelines.
column9: Generic VNF (implemented in experiments)..
column10: Mininet, OpenDayLight.
column11: Pre-deployment verification and static configuration checking.
column12: Virtual middleboxes are represented as stateful forwarding abstracts using match-action tables and Finite State Machines (FSMs), which are combined with topological switch forwarding rules to construct a Stateful Forwarding Graph (SFG) that SFC-Checker traverses to statically audit path reachability and policy constraints.
column14: OpenFlow switch flow tables from SDN controllers and middlebox state machines with match-action rules.
column15: Flow table and VNF states.
column19: OpenFlow protocol, OpenDayLight controller.
column24: Developed a 2279-line Java prototype that verifies stateful SFC forwarding rules by combining OpenFlow match-action tables and middlebox Finite State Machines into a Stateful Forwarding Graph. Scalability benchmarks demonstrated that Stateful Forwarding Graph construction time ranged from 5.5 ms to 7.9 ms across OpenDayLight SFC L2, OpenDayLight SFC NSH, and ContextNet implementations, while path forwarding checking across 1800 network functions per path took 12 ms. Evaluating Query 1 across per-network function state spaces increased checking time from 8 ms for 2 states to 1 second for 27 states, and 20 seconds for 52 states per network function. On a ContextNet commercial testbed topology with 4 switches and 15 network functions, SFC-Checker built the 112-node Stateful Forwarding Graph in 8 ms and verified stateful reachability in 15 ms.
column25: Limitations explicitly stated by the authors note that Finite State Machine forwarding models for evaluated middleboxes were constructed manually rather than extracted automatically from source code or binaries. Methodological limitations include strictly verifying Layer 2 and Layer 3 stateful forwarding behavior and reachability invariants while ignoring non-forwarding middlebox functions such as payload modifications, deep content optimization, and performance counting.
column26: Explicitly identified by the authors, automated extraction and synthesis of abstract stateful forwarding models directly from middlebox source code, configurations, or binaries remains an open problem. Inferred from the article, real-time verification under high-frequency runtime state changes without full offline Stateful Forwarding Graph re-computation requires further development.
column27: The authors concluded that integrating network routing rules and middlebox state machine abstractions into a Stateful Forwarding Graph allows static reachability analysis to verify complex stateful service chains in sub-second timeframes prior to live network deployment. Future work proposed by the authors includes developing automated mechanisms for generating network function forwarding models, validating the abstract state model on a broader set of commercial middleboxes, and extending the framework to real-time verification by reactively pulling runtime states from active network functions.

column1: A Benchmarking Methodology For Virtualized Packet Core Implementations
column6: Performance evaluation and benchmarking of virtualized packet cores (vEPC). The authors argue that conventional "black-box" testing methodologies are inadequate for NFV because software components share underlying physical cloud infrastructure. They argue that benchmarking must explicitly correlate network-level service quality (KPIs) with host-level system resource consumption.
column7: To define and validate a standardized benchmarking methodology that measures KPIs across workloads, lifecycle operations, and cloud-native capabilities (like elasticity and reliability) to identify software bottlenecks and optimize virtual packet core deployments.
column8: The research approach defines a holistic, cross-layer benchmarking paradigm that correlates system resource consumption with network-level service quality to evaluate virtualized network functions. The methodology develops a standardized testing framework that measures Key Parameter Indicators (KPIs) across workload, lifecycle, elasticity, and reliability dimensions, validating the approach through automated bottleneck detection tests executed on the Open5GCore toolkit.
column9: Virtualized Evolved Packet Core (vEPC) components including Mobility Management Entity (MME) and data plane switches (implemented in experiments).
column10: Open5GCore toolkit, VMWare Virtual Machines.
column11: Pre-deployment benchmarking and performance optimization.
column12: Software-only packet core functions share a shared cloud data center infrastructure; an automated benchmarking tool emulates eNBs and up to 20,000 UEs to execute spike and stress testing, correlating service quality metrics (session losses and delay) with compute/network resource metrics (vCPU and memory) to discover software bottlenecks.
column14: An NFV monitoring tool collecting service quality metrics from emulated 3GPP Evolved Packet Core subscriber traffic alongside system resource utilization from data center virtual machines.
column15: End-to-end service delay, packet delay variation, jitter, data packet loss percentage, CPU usage, memory usage, disk usage, subscriber procedures executed per second, active subscriber count, and throughput.
column19: Fraunhofer FOKUS Open5GCore toolkit, 3GPP EPC protocols, LTE cell emulation tools, user mobility emulators, and virtual machine monitor tools.
column24: Evaluated Fraunhofer FOKUS Open5GCore deployed on OpenStack using an automated benchmarking framework correlating service Key Parameter Indicators with cloud resource utilization. In attachment stress testing with 4 vCPUs, the system was stable from 0 to 30 attachments per second with 45 to 50 ms delay and zero session loss, and between 40 and 70 attachments per second with up to 100 ms delay and minimal loss, but exhibited system instability and severe session loss above 70 attachments per second as CPU utilization reached 100%, while memory consumption remained minimal at under 128 MB. In control plane scaling with 2 vCPUs per controller, scaling triggered at 50 attachments per second with scale-out and scale-in management latencies of 10 ms and 1 ms respectively, stabilizing service Key Parameter Indicators within 1 second and incurring a 1% CPU overhead for state synchronization. Data path performance evaluations showed that uniform low latency on the data plane could not be achieved without specialized hardware or software acceleration libraries.
column25: Limitations explicitly stated by the authors note that the benchmarking methodology lacks automated identification of system instability points, relying instead on human inspection of plotted data, and that memory management in the tested virtual evolved packet core implementation was overly restrictive, consuming excessive CPU cycles to keep memory usage low. Methodological limitations include conducting benchmark evaluations on a single physical host data center setup without testing multi-datacenter geo-distributed core network topologies.
column26: Explicitly identified by the authors, there is a lack of standardized industry methodologies for benchmarking virtualized connectivity services that correlate end-to-end subscriber service quality with cloud infrastructure resource overhead. Inferred from the article, benchmarking under complex subscriber mobility patterns, idle-mode state transitions, and extreme edge-cloud resource contention requires further formalization.
column27: The authors concluded that software-only virtual evolved packet core solutions exhibit non-linear resource consumption where CPU is the primary bottleneck rather than memory or disk, making automated benchmarking that correlates subscriber-perceived Key Parameter Indicators with cloud resource consumption essential for cloud-native core network deployment. Future work proposed by the authors includes redesigning virtual evolved packet core software architectures to utilize memory more aggressively to reduce CPU overhead, incorporating acceleration libraries, extending the benchmarking tool to emulate idle-mode subscriber devices and long-duration high-capacity test cycles, and contributing toward an ETSI standard for virtual network function benchmarking.

column1: Self-Modeling Based Diagnosis Of Services Over Programmable Networks
column6: Multi-layer fault diagnosis in dynamic, software-defined networks. The authors argue that the highly programmable and constantly changing nature of SDN/NFV environments introduces high diagnostic uncertainty. They argue that dynamic, on-the-fly dependency mapping (linking physical, logical, virtual, and service layers) is required to perform precise root-cause analysis.
column7: To propose a self-modeling diagnosis framework that automatically generates dependency templates and employs a Bayesian Network-based root-cause analysis to pinpoint failures down to highly specific internal components (such as specific CPUs or ports).
column8: The research approach is a dynamic, self-modeling diagnostic paradigm designed to automate fault isolation in highly programmable and constantly changing network architectures. The methodology employs extendable, machine-readable templates to construct dynamic dependency graphs mapping physical, logical, virtual, and service layers, which are subsequently analyzed using a Bayesian Network-based root-cause analysis to pinpoint malfunctions down to specific fine-grained internal elements like specific CPUs or ports.
column9: VPN, NAT, Firewall, video streaming (evaluated in simulation).
column10: SDN controller (OpenDaylight/OpenFlow) (hypervisor technology Not presented).
column11: Runtime online self-diagnosis and fault-localization.
column12: VNF instances are placed inside hosts and connected through virtual paths established by an SDN controller; they are mapped into a physical-logical-virtual-service dependency graph using fine-grained templates, allowing a Bayesian Network root-cause analysis module to correlate alarms and localize failure elements (CPUs, ports, or applications) on-the-fly.
column14: Network detection scripts collecting physical, logical, virtual, and service layer observations across SDN controllers, virtual switches, hosts, network interfaces, and VNF instances.
column15: Fault probabilities, component failure states, CPU load, and throughput.
column19: Bayesian Networks, OpenFlow protocol, OpenDaylight controller with SFC module, NFV records, and detection scripts.
column24: Evaluated a multi-layer self-diagnosis framework combining fine-grained structural templates, automated self-modeling, and Bayesian Networks across linear and meshed SDN and NFV topologies in OpenDaylight and OpenStack environments. Model execution timing showed that self-modeling time accounted for over 51% of total diagnosis time, and adding 6 networking services increased self-modeling time by 57% and root-cause analysis time by 72%, demonstrating that the Bayesian Network reasoning engine scales worse than the self-modeling graph generation algorithm. Service-aware scope reduction in a linear topology with 5 nodes reduced graph size from 196 vertices and 592 edges down to 111 vertices and 350 edges when scoping diagnosis strictly to the affected service region, cutting total diagnosis time in half from 4.0 seconds to 2.1 seconds.
column25: Limitations explicitly stated by the authors note that Bayesian Network inference computational complexity grows significantly as the number of cross-layer dependencies and concurrent services increases, creating scalability bottlenecks for large-scale topologies. Methodological limitations include dependency templates and conditional probability tables requiring precise initial domain modeling to avoid diagnosis bias.
column26: Explicitly identified by the authors, there is a lack of root-cause diagnosis frameworks covering combined SDN control and data plane elements alongside virtualized service layers in dynamic programmable networks. Inferred from the article, predictive fault prevention prior to alarm generation based on real-time performance degradation metrics remains unaddressed.
column27: The authors concluded that automated on-the-fly self-modeling combined with service-aware Bayesian Network reasoning successfully localizes fine-grained root causes across physical, logical, virtual, and service layers while reducing diagnosis uncertainty and graph processing overhead. Future work proposed by the authors includes developing an automated anomaly detection module to evaluate the performance impact of resource degradations such as CPU load spikes and throughput drops on virtual network functions to predict and prevent future failures.

column1: Answer: Combining Nfv And Sdn Features For Network Resilience Strategies
column6: Network resilience and real-time security mitigation (e.g., against DDoS attacks). The authors argue that neither SDN nor NFV can provide optimal security in isolation. They argue that combining the global visibility of SDN controllers with the rapid, on-demand scalability of NFV-deployed security functions (like firewalls and IDSs) creates a powerful, closed feedback loop for threat suppression.
column7: To present ANSwer, an integrated architecture that establishes a feedback control-loop to monitor network behavior, dynamically identify anomalies, and rapidly reconfigure or scale defense functions to protect network availability with minimal resource footprint.
column8: The research approach is an integrated security feedback control-loop paradigm that combines the central control of SDN with the dynamic deployment capabilities of NFV to enhance network resilience. The methodology implements "ANSwer", a system that continuously monitors network behavior to detect anomalies like DDoS attacks and dynamically reconfigures or scales security VNFs (such as firewalls and intrusion detection systems) on-demand to suppress malicious traffic while minimizing resource footprint.
column9: Virtual Firewall (vFirewall), Virtual IDS/IPS (vIDS/IPS), Virtual Honeypot (vHoneypot), Virtual Monitor (vMonitor), Virtual Controller (vController) (implemented in experiments); Deep Packet Inspection (DPI), Anti-virus, Anti-spam (cited as examples).

column14: The vMonitor component and SDN controller collecting OpenFlow switch flow stats, link status, and ICMP probing data across network devices and virtualized security functions.
column15: Packets count, bytes count, mean and standard deviation of traffic flow volume, throughput, available bandwidth, link delay, and service response time.
column16: Security alert logs, anomaly event logs, and traffic profiling logs recorded by vIDS/IPS, vFirewall, and vHoneyPot.

Control-loop baseline training established anomaly detection thresholds at 10% above moving standard deviation of traffic flow metrics. In real-time threat mitigation testing against SYN flood and DDoS attacks, the framework dynamically rerouted suspicious flows through virtual IDS/IPS and virtual honeypot via OpenFlow rule modifications and deployed host isolation rules when virtual network functions were overwhelmed, successfully maintaining service availability.
column25: Limitations explicitly stated by the authors note that the evaluated set of combined SDN and NFV resilience strategies represents only a subset of possible feature combinations, and that the prototype relies on statistical standard deviation thresholds that require pre-training. Methodological limitations include executing experiments in a Mininet emulated environment on a single physical host rather than a multi-node production cloud data center.
column26: Explicitly identified by the authors, optimal selection and dynamic composition of resilience strategies under complex, multi-vector attacks without manual rule definition remains an open challenge. Inferred from the article, evaluation of control-loop signaling overhead and state synchronization latency across multi-controller federated SDN and NFV domains is missing.
column27: The authors concluded that combining global SDN visibility and flow control with elastic virtual network function deployment creates an adaptive, closed-loop network resilience architecture capable of identifying and mitigating network traffic anomalies in real time. Future work proposed by the authors includes incorporating additional virtual network functions such as load balancers, deep packet inspection, and anti-virus, exploring reinforcement learning algorithms to enhance feedback control-loop decision making, and extending the architecture to support disruption tolerance and advanced security aspects.

column1: Enabling Agile Video Transcoding Over Sdn/Nfv-Enabled Networks
column6: Quality of Experience (QoE) management for mobile video streaming. The authors argue that rigid, hardware-based transcoders cannot dynamically adapt to localized, transient network congestion. They argue that dynamic, software-driven Service Function Chaining (SFC) allows for the agile, on-demand deployment of transcoding instances closer to the user to prevent buffering.
column7: To implement a proof-of-concept system over an SDN-NFV network that detects localized congestion and dynamically deploys a transcoder VNF to seamlessly lower video bitrates, preserving user QoE without service interruption.
column8: The research approach employs a dynamic content delivery and Quality of Experience (QoE) preservation paradigm to resolve localized network congestion. The methodology designs a proof-of-concept orchestration system that combines SDN and NFV to detect user-side congestion in real-time and dynamically deploys and routes video traffic through a transcoder VNF using Service Function Chaining to lower streaming bitrates without service disruption.
column9: Video transcoding and real-time media adaptation process (implemented in experiments).
column10: OpenStack cloud platform, Open Virtual Switches, and OpenDaylight SDN controller.
column11: Dynamic runtime instantiation, on-the-fly resource allocation, and automated routing.
column12: Integrated at an edge NFVI Point of Presence to dynamically transcode unicast video streams down to lower bitrates, bypassing access link bottlenecks to restore user Quality of Experience seamlessly.

column1: A Connectionist Approach To Dynamic Resource Management For Virtualised Network Functions
column6: Dynamic, autonomous resource allocation and scaling for Virtualized Network Functions (VNFs). The authors argue that since network traffic traverses VNFs sequentially in a Service Function Chain (SFC), the resource requirements of any given VNF depend on the resource states of its neighbors in the chain. Traditional static or manual allocation, as well as independent reinforcement learning, fails to capture these topological dependencies. A topology-aware connectionist approach leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can exploit sequence information to predict resource demands accurately before congestion occurs.

column8: The research approach leverages a topology-aware connectionist paradigm to predict and automate VNF resource scaling within sequential Service Function Chains. The methodology utilizes a Graph Neural Network (GNN) algorithm that analyzes the historical performance data of individual VNF components alongside the topological interdependencies of adjacent components in a service chain, validated on a virtualized IP Multimedia Subsystem (vIMS).

column1: Efficient Detection Of Flow Anomalies With Limited Monitoring Resources
column6: Real-time detection of network flow anomalies (e.g., heavy hitters, SYN floods) in Cloud and NFV environments under strict hardware resource constraints. The authors argue that because physical switch counters (e.g., TCAM entries) are severely limited compared to the massive number of active flows, instantaneous and perfectly accurate anomaly detection is mathematically impossible. However, operators can trade off immediate detection for absolute accuracy by identifying anomaly-producing flows over a constant number of evaluation rounds (epochs).
column7: To formalize the resource-time trade-off in network monitoring and propose "IPv4 Prefixing", a provably accurate, multi-round monitoring algorithm that dynamically adjusts the aggregation prefix/CIDR masks of flow counters to isolate and pinpoint the exact source of a flow anomaly with minimal counters.
column8: The research approach investigates the trade-off between monitoring speed and hardware efficiency to execute exact network anomaly identification under severe resource constraints. The methodology implements an "IPv4 prefixing" algorithm that maps active flows into a hierarchical trie structure and dynamically zooms in on suspicious traffic aggregates by refining and folding flowsets based on usage thresholds, offloading this monitoring logic directly into network switches to achieve accurate anomaly detection within approximately three seconds.

Evaluated using Open vSwitch, Ryu controller, and replayed CAIDA real-life traffic traces under Heavy Hitter and SYN flood anomaly injections. Verified that the algorithm identifies exact anomalous flows within 3 to 4 seconds or epochs using only a few counters, regardless of total flow volume. Compared two SDN deployment schemes: the Pushing Scheme executing monitoring logic directly inside the switch via OpenFlow Experimenter messages and the Polling Scheme with logic in the controller polling counters. The Pushing Scheme reduced control plane communication overhead dramatically and eliminated controller processing delay without imposing observable CPU or memory overhead on the switch.

column27: The authors concluded that flow anomalies can be accurately detected with very limited counter resources by allowing a 3 to 4 second detection window, and executing monitoring logic directly inside SDN switches significantly outperforms controller polling in communication overhead and reaction speed for local switch traffic. column1: Openbox: A Software-Defined Framework For Developing, Deploying, And Managing Network Functions
column6: Decoupling the control plane of Network Functions (NFs/middleboxes) from their packet-processing data plane. The authors argue that while Software-Defined Networking (SDN) has successfully decoupled forwarding appliances (switches/routers), NFs remain monolithic, expensive, and proprietary. They argue that many distinct NFs perform highly similar underlying packet-processing steps (e.g., header classification, regular expression matching); thus, logically centralizing the control plane allows the network to merge multiple NF application graphs to execute redundant steps only once per packet, drastically improving throughput and latency.
column7: To present and evaluate OpenBox, a software-defined framework consisting of a logically centralized OpenBox Controller (OBC), basic general-purpose packet-processing elements called OpenBox Instances (OBIs), a declarative northbound programming API, and an open communication protocol to deploy, scale, and merge multi-tenant NF policies network-wide.
column8: The research approach utilizes a software-defined decoupling paradigm to separate the centralized control plane of network middleboxes from their underlying packet-processing data planes. The methodology introduces "OpenBox", which deploys a logically centralized controller to orchestrate standardized OpenBox Instances (OBIs), merging the processing logic of multiple distinct network functions into a single, optimized path to execute computationally heavy operations like classification only once per packet.

column1: U-Haul: Efficient State Migration In Nfv
column6: Optimizing internal state migration across VNF instances during dynamic load balancing. The authors argue that existing state-transfer frameworks (such as OpenNF) cause substantial downtime and control-plane overhead because they blindly transfer states for all active flows. Highlighting that real-world network traffic is heavily dominated by short-lived "mice" flows, they argue that these mice flows will naturally complete and expire before the migration process itself concludes. Thus, the system should only migrate states for long-lived "elephant" flows while leaving mice flows to expire on the source instance.
column7: To design and implement U-HAUL, an efficient state-migration system that introduces a lightweight Traffic Proportion based Elephant Detection Module (EDM) at each VNF, coupled with a filter API, to migrate only elephant flow states and minimize migration downtime, controller buffering, and mice flow completion times.
column8: The research approach establishes a selective state-transfer paradigm to optimize VNF state migration during dynamic load balancing in data centers. The methodology introduces "U-HAUL", a system that distinguishes between short-lived "mice" flows and long-lived "elephant" flows, applying a policy to migrate only the states of elephant flows while letting mice flows expire naturally on their original instances to reduce migration downtime.

For mice flows, U-HAUL reduced flow completion time latency by at least 78.3% for web search traffic, 94.5% for Facebook cache traffic, and 97.6% for Azure WAN traffic. Traffic-proportion-based elephant flow detection achieved an average accuracy of 95.0% on web search, 94.9% on Facebook, and 87.5% on Azure WAN workloads, outperforming traditional size-based detection threshold approaches.

column1: Extensible Framework For Elastic Orchestration Of Service Function Chains In 5G Networks
column6: Elastic, dynamic, and resilient orchestration of Service Function Chains (SFCs) in 5G SGi-LAN networks. column6: Forwarding verification and auditing of Service Function Chains (SFCs) hosted on third-party clouds. Future work proposed by the authors includes further analyzing the cost function equation to study parameter impacts on optimal configurations, investigating whether the cost function shows a bias toward centralized or distributed mechanisms across the configuration space, and extending the cost function with metrics that quantify developer ease-of-use for both centralized and distributed architectures.

column1: Arav: Monitoring A Cloud'S Virtual Routers
column6: Security monitoring of virtual routers (VRs) in multi-tenant cloud data centers. The authors argue that virtual routers are highly vulnerable to targeted attacks, yet traditional agent-based security monitoring is completely incompatible with VRs because of their ephemeral nature, stripped-down guest operating systems, and placement in the cloud. To overcome these challenges, they argue that cloud providers should leverage virtualization itself to monitor VRs from the hypervisor level. Fusing Virtual Machine Introspection (VMI) with instruction-level breakpoint injection allows the monitoring system to trace guest process-level function calls and extract rich application context directly from registers, bypassing the need for in-guest agents.
column7: To design, implement, and evaluate Arav, a hypervisor-based security monitoring system that injects memory breakpoints to trace guest VR function calls, reconstruct security events, and mitigate attacks on services (such as Quagga and OpenVPN) in real time with negligible performance overhead.
column8: The research approach implements an agentless security monitoring paradigm that shifts threat detection from the virtual machine guest level to the underlying hypervisor layer. The methodology designs "Arav", a framework that uses Virtual Machine Introspection (VMI) combined with instruction-level breakpoint injection at the hypervisor level to trace guest process-level function calls, capturing rich security events such as credential guessing and resource exhaustion.
column9: Virtual Routers running OSPF dynamic routing via the Quagga daemon and VPN concentrator via the OpenVPN service (implemented in experiments); NAT, dynamic routing, and firewalling (cited as examples).
column10: Xen hypervisor (specifically Domain 0), LibVMI library, and guest virtual machines running pfSense (FreeBSD) and VyOS (Debian Linux).
column11: Runtime security monitoring, guest process function-call tracing, anomaly detection, threat mitigation, and automated service recovery via VM reboots.
column12: Arav runs as a privileged process in the hypervisor (Xen Domain 0) and uses Virtual Machine Introspection to inject instruction-level breakpoints into the active memory of virtual routers. When a process (such as Quagga or OpenVPN) triggers a breakpoint, the hypervisor suspends the VR, allowing Arav to extract register arguments, reconstruct guest process-level security events, and dynamically inject firewall blocks or trigger VM reboots without guest-side agents.
column14: Hypervisor-based virtual machine introspection monitoring process-level function calls, guest vCPU registers, and memory across pfSense and VyOS virtual routers.
column15: vCPU registers and memory.
column16: In-guest function call logs, security event logs, and alert logs reconstituted from guest process execution traces.
column17: Sequential streams of process-level function calls and vCPU register state entries captured via breakpoint injection to infer security events.
column18: Arav maps sequential function call traces and vCPU register state entries directly to security event logs.
column19: Virtual Machine Introspection, LibVMI library, Xen hypervisor, breakpoint injection.
column24: Developed Arav, an agentless security monitoring framework for cloud virtual routers (VRs) using hypervisor-level Virtual Machine Introspection (VMI) and breakpoint injection. Evaluated Arav on pfSense and VyOS virtual routers running OpenVPN and Quagga daemons. Arav successfully reconstituted process function calls into security events, detecting threats such as credential guessing and resource exhaustion attacks. Performance evaluation showed that Arav incurred a negligible execution overhead of less than 0.63% on virtual router throughput. Breakpoint injection evaluation demonstrated a recall rate of 1.0 with zero false positives when security event generators were properly configured.
column25: Limitations explicitly stated by the authors note that Arav modifies virtual router memory by replacing executable code bytes with breakpoints, which can be detected by guest anti-debugging or kernel integrity checking mechanisms because Arav does not currently conceal injected breakpoints. Methodological limitations include requiring access to virtual router debugging symbols or unstripped binaries to map function names to memory offsets, which may be unavailable for proprietary virtual routers.
column26: Explicitly identified by the authors, monitoring ephemeral virtual routers without installing in-guest software agents remains difficult in cloud environments. Inferred from the article, extracting function-to-memory mappings for closed-source proprietary virtual routers without debugging symbols remains an open problem.
column27: The authors concluded that hypervisor-based Virtual Machine Introspection with breakpoint injection enables non-intrusive, agentless security monitoring of cloud virtual routers, achieving high event detection recall with negligible performance overhead. Future work was not explicitly proposed by the authors beyond discussing future adoption of breakpoint concealment techniques to prevent guest anti-debugging detection.

column1: Jaal: Towards Network Intrusion Detection At Isp Scale
column6: Scalable network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) in wide area networks (WANs) and ISP-scale environments. The authors argue that enterprise-scale NIDS architectures fail at the ISP scale because continuously transferring copies of raw packets to a central engine for deep packet inspection consumes too much bandwidth and causes severe packet loss (over 50% at speeds exceeding 20 Gbps). They contend that a scalable NIDS must shift to a hybrid approach: local monitors extract concise, lower-dimensional "packet summaries" using clustering, and a centralized engine processes these summaries to detect distributed WAN-wide attacks.
column7: To present and evaluate Jaal, a modular ISP-scale NIDS that performs in-network packet summarization, automatically transforms enterprise-class signature rules (e.g., Snort rules) to evaluate summaries, and detects coordinated distributed attacks with high accuracy while reducing communication overhead.
column8: The research approach is a hybrid, distributed threat-detection paradigm designed to execute wide-area network security monitoring at an Internet Service Provider (ISP) scale. The methodology implements "Jaal", an intrusion detection framework that performs in-network packet summarization via dimensionality reduction techniques like Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and K-means clustering, translating standardized signature rules to evaluate these summaries and utilizing a feedback loop to request raw packets only during high-precision verification phases.

These monitors extract headers of passing packets in real-time, compute lightweight summaries using dimensionality reduction (SVD and K-means), and transmit them to a centralized inference engine that executes equivalent Snort-style rules, minimizing WAN bandwidth overhead while maintaining a global threat visibility.
column14: Network monitors deployed across ISP routers extracting packet headers and building low-dimensional packet summaries.
column15: TCP/IP headers (18 header fields).

column19: Snort IDS rules, OpenFlow.

Evaluated Jaal on a testbed simulating large WAN topologies under SYN flood, Sockstress, port scan, and distributed SSH brute force attacks. Compared against conventional centralized NIDS that copy raw packets, which caused a 70% throughput drop and 75% accuracy loss under high traffic. Jaal achieved an average true positive rate of approximately 98% at a 9% false positive rate while reducing communication overhead by 65% compared to raw packet mirroring.
column25: Limitations explicitly stated by the authors note that generating in-network packet summaries introduces a trade-off where extreme dimensionality reduction can increase false positive rates, requiring careful tuning of summarization parameters. Methodological limitations include relying on two-step matrix reduction approximations rather than joint multi-mode optimization due to computational intractability.

Inferred from the article, dynamic retrieval of raw packet traces upon summary alert detection to eliminate false positives in production ISP environments requires further evaluation.
column27: The authors concluded that replacing raw packet mirroring with in-network dimensionality reduction summaries allows intrusion detection systems to scale to ISP-level traffic, preserving flow correlations and maintaining high detection accuracy (~98%) with drastically reduced bandwidth overhead. Future work proposed by the authors includes exploring finer-grained summary requests or raw packet retrievals when alerts are raised to further reduce false positive rates, and investigating random retrieval of full packet traces upon attack flagging.

column6: Automated Virtual Network Function (VNF) onboarding, profiling, and elastic resource configuration. column1: Sciencesds: A Novel Software Defined Security Framework For Large-Scale Data- Intensive Science
column6: Cybersecurity provisioning in data-intensive scientific networks (Science DMZs). transfers (SNAG) classification mechanism to bypass trusted science flows while dynamically steering untrusted traffic through inspection VNFs.

column1: Sketchvisor: Robust Network Measurement For Software Packet Processing
column6: High-performance, robust network measurement within software switches. The authors argue that while sketch-based measurement algorithms offer strong theoretical guarantees, applying them directly within software packet processing engines consumes excessive CPU resources and causes severe throughput degradation under high traffic loads. They argue that software switches should be augmented with a "fast path", activated only during traffic spikes or overloads, which tracks large flows with low-overhead, top-k data structures, while a centralized controller reconstructs full network-wide measurement statistics from both the sketch and fast path results.
column7: To design, implement, and evaluate SketchVisor, a robust network-wide software switch measurement framework that utilizes a lightweight top-k fast path to process overflow packets and leverages compressive-sensing-based matrix interpolation in the control plane to recover accurate network-wide traffic statistics.
column8: The research approach utilizes a dual-path software packet processing paradigm to execute robust, high-performance traffic measurements during severe network congestion. The methodology introduces "SketchVisor", which deploys a fast-path architecture equipped with a lightweight top-k algorithm to track large flows under heavy CPU loads, and leverages compressive-sensing-based matrix interpolation at the centralized control plane to recover highly accurate, network-wide traffic statistics.
column9: Large flow tracking, network traffic measurement, heavy hitter detection, heavy changer detection, DDoS detection, and entropy measurement (implemented in experiments).
column10: Open vSwitch.

column12: Embedded directly into software switches across multiple hosts in the data plane under operator control. Excessive traffic exceeding the processing capacity of the normal sketch path is redirected to a lightweight fast path top-k tracking algorithm to maintain line-rate throughput without packet dropping during congestion, while a centralized controller recovers network-wide statistics via compressive sensing matrix interpolation.
column14: Distributed software switches running sketch-based measurement modules alongside a fast-path top-k flow module and a centralized control plane.
column15: Heavy hitter, heavy changer, DDoS, superspreader, cardinality, flow size distribution, entropy.
column19: Open vSwitch, FlowRadar, RevSketch, UnivMon, Deltoid, TwoLevel, FM, kMin, LC, MRAC.
column24: Evaluated SketchVisor prototype integrated with Open vSwitch across a 9-host testbed and an in-memory tester for various measurement tasks including heavy hitter detection, heavy changer detection, DDoS detection, superspreader detection, cardinality estimation, flow size distribution, and entropy estimation. SketchVisor achieved over 10 Gbps throughput per CPU core on the testbed and over 17 Gbps throughput on the in-memory tester, reaching up to 40 Gbps for MRAC, while baseline sketch solutions without a fast path achieved only 1.32 Gbps to 6.41 Gbps. Network-wide recovery using compressive sensing restored measurement accuracy close to ideal sketch performance processing all traffic, achieving above 90% recall and 84% precision for DDoS detection, nearly perfect recall for superspreader detection, and reducing heavy hitter relative errors to near-ideal levels across 1 to 128 hosts. Fast path top-k tracking redirected 20% to 50% of overloaded flows while consuming only 8 KB of memory and 47 CPU cycles per packet update.

Future work proposed by the authors includes evaluating SketchVisor in kernel-bypass environments such as DPDK, parallelizing the compressive sensing solver across multiple CPU cores, and conducting theoretical analysis of average-case error bounds for the top-k tracking algorithm.

column1: Flexnfv: Flexible Network Service Chaining With Dynamic Scaling
column6: Dynamic runtime scaling and performance optimization for virtualized network service chains operating in multi-core environments. The authors argue that service chains behave fundamentally differently from monolithic NFs because heterogeneous NF processing costs mean satisfying one NF's capacity does not guarantee that subsequent NFs won't become bottlenecks. They contend that high-performance user-space I/O frameworks like DPDK require an active chain-level regulatory mechanism to prevent buffer overflows, and that horizontal dynamic core scaling outperforms CPU-share scheduling platforms (such as NFVnice).

Built upon a DPDK based framework, FlexNFV aims to perform timely NF scaling driven by real-time, chain-level telemetry, combining per packet processing costs, traffic arrival rates, total NF load, and inter-NF queue lengths, to evenly distribute workloads across instances and prevent performance degradation such as packet drops at bottleneck NFs.
column8: The research approach is to optimize execution through a launching avoidance strategy that reinstates blocked instances rather than spawning new ones, uses DPDK P-states to lower CPU frequency during underloaded periods, and assigns dedicated per-instance message queues to prevent control conflicts. The methodology is implement FlexNFV on OpenNetVM by decoupling system responsibilities into a primary manager process for packet routing and telemetry, and secondary NF processes running on dedicated CPU cores. They developed an abstraction library (scalib) that monitors chain-level metrics against set watermarks to trigger automated scaling.

column12: Deployed as secondary DPDK processes running on dedicated physical CPU cores managed by a primary DPDK NF Manager process with zero-copy shared memory packet delivery. The FlexNFV scalib library calculates real-time NF load using per-packet timestamps and queue lengths; when overload occurs, it rapidly spawns child NF instances or reinstates blocked instances on idle cores, using DPDK P-states APIs to lower CPU core frequencies during blocked states to save power without incurring exit latencies.
column14: FlexNFV manager status and Scaling threads periodically polling DPDK shared memory ring queues and per-NF load counters across service chains.

column24: Evaluated on a testbed with two Dell servers (Dell R730 generating 64-byte packets via Pktgen-DPDK and Dell R740 running FlexNFV on OpenNetVM with DPDK v18.05). In a 3-NF service chain (Monitor NF1, Forwarder NF2, AES Encryptor NF3), FlexNFV doubled service chain throughput compared to OpenNetVM when the input rate reached 6 Gbps, maintaining linear throughput growth up to theoretical line rate without packet drops. In contrast, OpenNetVM experienced heavy packet drops on NF1 (dropping up to 4.63 Mpps at 6 Gbps input rate) and hit a performance ceiling at 3 Gbps input rate. FlexNFV demonstrated load-aware flexibility under sudden traffic fluctuations: when input traffic dropped from 4 Gbps to 2 Gbps, FlexNFV immediately blocked redundant NF instances and set their CPU cores to minimum frequency via P-states power management. When traffic resurged to 4 Gbps, FlexNFV reinstated blocked instances via launching avoidance rather than launching new ones, eliminating packet drops after a brief transient. Scaling latency for instantiating new NFs averaged 998 ms. In a head-to-head comparison with NFVnice on a 3-NF chain under line-rate traffic, FlexNFV achieved 1.13 Mpps higher throughput, representing a 17.5 percent performance improvement over NFVnice.

column1: Nfvnice: Dynamic Backpressure And Scheduling For Nfv Service Chains
column6: Managing network function service chains on commodity hardware requires efficient system resource allocation and CPU scheduling. The authors argue that traditional operating system schedulers operate along application agnostic dimensions and lack packet level metrics, preventing them from allocating processing time in proportion to packet arrival rates and heterogeneous computational costs. In densely packed containerized environments, downstream bottleneck functions drop packets after upstream functions have already expended CPU cycles on them, causing severe receive livelock and wasting processing capacity. Frequent context switches enforced by default operating system schedulers disrupt CPU cache locality, significantly increasing processing latency and latency variance across service chains. Achieving high throughput and predictable latency does not require modifying the operating system kernel, as user space monitoring can translate queue telemetry into standard process scheduling abstractions and dynamic backpressure controls.
column7: To design, implement, and evaluate NFVnice, an operating system independent user space management and resource scheduling framework for virtualized network function service chains on DPDK based platforms. The framework automatically measures packet arrival rates and execution service times per network function to dynamically compute CPU shares, ensuring rate cost proportional fairness across heterogeneous workloads.
column8: The research approach evaluates the NFVnice framework on top of the OpenNetVM and DPDK platforms running in user space on commodity multi-core hardware. It employs a dedicated user-space monitoring thread operating a lightweight library named libnf to sample packet arrival rates, execution cycle costs, and queue occupancy via hardware counters and shared memory histograms. Rather than modifying the operating system kernel, the framework translates these measured processing loads into dynamic CPU share allocations updated every 10 milliseconds using Linux cgroup controls. The methodology considered a benchmark on a physical dual-socket Intel Xeon server testbed with 10Gbps DPDK interfaces using Moongen, Pktgen, and Iperf3 traffic generators against standard Linux schedulers across throughput, latency distributions, CPU utilization, and packet drop metrics.
column9: Firewall, Network Address Translation (NAT), Proxy, Deep Packet Inspection (DPI), WAN Optimizer (cited as examples). Traffic Monitor, Load Balancer, AES Encryption, VLAN Tagging (Implemented in experiments).
column10: OpenNetVM user-space platform, DPDK, Docker containers.
column11: Process scheduling, backpressure throttling, runtime load regulation.
column12: Integrated as chained user-space network functions linked via libnf and DPDK shared memory ring buffers on shared or dedicated CPU cores where a monitoring thread measures packet processing cycles to dynamically update cgroup weights and enforce selective cross-chain backpressure.
column14: DPDK shared memory ring buffers and libnf user-space cycle counters measuring packet processing execution times and queue occupancy.
column15: Per network function packet arrival rate, packet processing service time in CPU cycles, inter-function queue length, queuing delay, throughput in million packets per second, packet drop rate, round trip latency, context switch frequency, instructions per cycle.
column19: DPDK API, OpenNetVM shared memory ring buffers, libnf user-space library, hardware CPU cycle counters (RDTSC), Linux cgroups sysfs interface, Explicit Congestion Notification protocol.
column24: Evaluated on a testbed of Intel Xeon CPU E5-2697 v3 servers running Linux kernel 3.19.0 lowlatency, using Moongen, Pktgen, and Iperf3 to generate 10 Gbps traffic and CAIDA real-world packet traces. In a 3-NF single-core service chain (Low, Medium, High processing cost), NFVnice increased throughput by up to 2x over default Linux kernel schedulers (CFS Normal, CFS Batch, Round Robin) and reduced packet drops from 3 Mpps down to near zero (0.01 Mpps) under overload conditions. On multi-core deployments with pinned NFs, NFVnice backpressure reduced upstream CPU utilization from 100 percent down to 11 percent (for Low cost) and 64 percent (for Medium cost) while preserving aggregate throughput, eliminating wasted work from packets dropped downstream. Across multi-chain setups, NFVnice improved bottleneck chain throughput by 2x by freeing upstream processing capacity. Evaluated on CAIDA internet traces, NFVnice improved multi-chain throughput by up to 60 percent over default schedulers and provided over 500x throughput improvement for Round Robin. In performance isolation tests sharing TCP and UDP flows, NFVnice protected TCP throughput from collapsing (maintaining 3.3 Gbps versus 10 to 30 Mbps without NFVnice) when competing against non-responsive UDP flows. Across longer service chains (lengths 1 to 10), NFVnice maintained throughput gains up to 70 percent on multi-core configurations, while reducing packet processing latency by 50 to 70 percent across all quartiles.
column25: Limitations explicitly stated by the authors note that variable per-packet processing costs within an NF lead to inaccurate processing cost estimates and suboptimal CPU weight assignments, requiring reliance on backpressure rather than cgroup weights alone. Additionally, measuring per-packet processing time using CPU cycle counters on every packet induces CPU pipeline flushes, forcing NFVnice to use 1 ms sampling histograms and 100 ms moving medians. For very long service chains exceeding 7 NFs multiplexed on a single core, throughput gains over default schedulers diminish. Methodological limitations include evaluating NFVnice on a 3-node local server cluster connected back-to-back without WAN network delay or physical switch hardware.
column26: Explicitly identified by the authors, standard operating system process schedulers lacked packet-level arrival rate and per-packet processing cost visibility, causing severe receive livelock, wasted work, and unfairness when scheduling heterogeneous VNF service chains on shared cores. Inferred from limitations, developing ultra-low-overhead, real-time per-packet cost profiling mechanisms that do not trigger CPU pipeline flushes or inaccuracies under high packet processing variance remains an open research gap.
column27: The authors concluded that combining user-space rate-cost proportional cgroup weight assignment with selective chain-wide backpressure enables NFVnice to eliminate wasted work, protect responsive flows, reduce latency by 50 to 70 percent, and double service chain throughput across various operating system schedulers. Future work was Not explicitly addressed in the article beyond suggesting potential applications to user-space thread schedulers and multi-host backpressure extensions.

column1: Reinforce: Achieving Efficient Failure Resiliency For Network Function Virtualization-Based Services
column6: High availability (HA) and failure resiliency for stateful VNF service chains. The authors argue that while commodity-based software network functions are highly prone to multi-layer failures, traditional VM-level replication or packet access logging introduces unacceptable performance degradation and latency overheads. They argue that the system can dramatically minimize normal-operation overhead by separating deterministic and non-deterministic packet processing. This allows the platform to use "lazy" state checkpointing for heavyweight application state combined with high-performance, pipelined commits of lightweight per-flow timestamps at fine timescales.
column7: To introduce REINFORCE, an integrated resiliency framework for DPDK-based network functions and service chains that leverages external synchrony, opportunistic batching, and multi-buffering to achieve fast, consistent recovery from software, server, and link failures.
column8: The research approach implements a high-performance resiliency and state-replication paradigm designed to protect software-based network functions from physical and logical failures. The methodology develops the "REINFORCE" framework, which minimizes system overhead during normal operations by separating deterministic and non-deterministic packet processing, applying external synchrony and lazy checkpointing to achieve sub-10-millisecond failover times at 10 Gbps line-rate speeds.
column9: Network Address Translator (NAT), Firewall, Deep Packet Inspection (DPI), Intrusion Detection System (IDS), Load Balancer, Quality of Service (QoS), and Basic Monitor (implemented in experiments).

column12: Stateful VNFs run as containers integrated with the DPDK-based OpenNetVM platform and linked via a custom libnf library. Active NFs process line-rate traffic while predecessor nodes append logical timestamps and log outgoing packets; when local software crashes or host/link failures are detected via BFD or Linux OS signals, REINFORCE executes sub-millisecond local failovers or sub-10ms remote chain-level failovers by replaying buffered packets from predecessor nodes and restoring deterministic/non-deterministic states on standby containers.

column24: Evaluated on an experimental testbed of five Intel Xeon CPU E5-2697 v3 servers running Ubuntu SMP Linux kernel 3.19.0-39-lowlatency connected back-to-back with dual-port 10Gbps DPDK-compatible NICs, driven by MoonGen, apache-bench, and wrk traffic tools using the DPDK-based OpenNetVM platform. Achieved local NF failure detection and failover within 150 microseconds incurring less than 1% performance overhead and adding less than 5 microseconds latency during normal operation. Remote chain-level failover across servers in a LAN was achieved within 10 ms or 5 ms as reported in summary sections, incurring less than 10% performance overhead and adding an average latency of approximately 400 microseconds with a worst-case latency of less than 1 ms. Maintained line-rate throughput around 13.5 Mpps for stateless and stateful NFs like DPI and Basic Monitor, outperforming Pico Replication and FTMB by two orders of magnitude in remote replication latency, and achieving performance comparable to baseline. For non-deterministic rates less frequent than once every 250 microseconds, REINFORCE provided near line-rate processing, though throughput dropped to 0.22 Mpps when non-deterministic updates occurred every 1 nanosecond. In HTTP download failover tests, servicing throughput showed only a 3% to 4% reduction during active failure and recovery.

column1: A Tenant-Based Two-Stage Approach To Auditing The Integrity Of Virtual Network Function Chains Hosted On Third-Party Clouds
column6: Trust, integrity auditing, and virtualization security in multi-tenant clouds. The authors argue that as tenants increasingly host their Virtual Network Function (VNF) chains on third-party clouds, severe integrity breaches can silently arise due to misconfigurations or malicious co-located tenants (e.g., redirecting forwarding rules to bypass firewalls or deep packet inspection). They contend that relying solely on the cloud provider for security auditing is insufficient because provider-level checks lack tenant-level contextual requirements. Furthermore, a tenant cannot directly audit the system due to restricted infrastructure access and the massive confidentiality risks associated with shipping raw provider logs to the tenant.

The second stage dynamically requests selective, anonymized provider-level logs (via tools like iCAT) and applies formal security verification (using NFVGuard) to confirm or reject anomalies.

column1: Strca: A Lightweight And Accurate Root Cause Analysis System Based On 5G Signalling Trace
column6: Automated fault localization, signaling trace analysis, and fault propagation in NFV-based 5GC networks. The authors argue that the massive scale of 5G core networks and the complex, many-to-many mappings between virtualized elements and underlying physical servers make manual root-cause analysis (RCA) impossible. Standard diagnostic systems rely on heavy resource-level performance counters that lack fine-grained visibility into service-level dependencies. Since signaling traces accurately document the step-by-step communications and interactions between virtual elements, they are the ideal data source for real-time anomaly detection and root-cause localization.
column7: To design and evaluate STRCA, the first lightweight root cause analysis system based entirely on 5G signaling traces. STRCA features a signaling parse module to reconstruct traces, a trace anomaly detection module that identifies abnormal edges using a Volatility metric, and an RCA engine that applies a novel AnomalyDegree metric and FP-Growth mining to successfully localize root-cause elements in a real-world commercial Huawei 5GC with 76.3% accuracy.
column8: The research approach utilizes a lightweight, signaling-trace-based diagnostic paradigm to execute rapid, real-time root-cause analysis and bypass the computational complexity of tracking multi-layer physical-virtual performance counters in 5G Core networks. The methodology implements "STRCA", which reconstructs raw packet streams into cohesive signaling traces, applies a volatility metric to isolate delay-based anomalies, and utilizes an AnomalyDegree formula alongside FP-Growth mining to successfully locate malfunctioning elements in active telecommunications core systems.

column1: Near Real-Time Anomaly Detection In Nfv Infrastructures Ii: From Sm To Agmp
column6: Near Real-Time (NRT) telemetry anomaly detection in high-performance virtualized telecommunication infrastructures. The authors argue that while telemetry monitoring produces massive streams of multi-dimensional indicators, detecting performance anomalies in near real-time is computationally challenging. They contend that rather than using heavy, complex models, anomaly detection can be designed around low-overhead algebraic operations. Furthermore, generalizing a CPU-centric single-metric detector to other critical indicators (Memory, Network) and collapsing its free parameters from 13 down to a single parameter drastically reduces false alarms.
column7: To extend a single-metric NRT anomaly detection algorithm to handle multi-metric data across Vodafone's large-scale NFV infrastructures, enhancing detection precision while maintaining minimal computational overhead.
column8: The research approach employs a streamlined, multi-metric algebraic prediction paradigm to execute near real-time anomaly detection in virtualized telecommunication infrastructures without requiring a training phase. The methodology refines a single-metric detector using logarithmic transformations to create the Logarithmic Simplified Simple Median (LogSSM), which is subsequently expanded into the Algebro-Geometric Multi-metric Predictor (AGMP) to analyze the geometric correlations between diverse resource indicators in a multidimensional space and suppress false alarms.
